title: Object Detection & Segmentation
blurb: Tests how detection and segmentation differ from classification, the R-CNN lineage, YOLO's single-shot approach, U-Net's skip connections and how they differ from ResNet's, IoU and non-max suppression, and what removing U-Net's skips cost.

refLinks.label: §70.2.1 The R-CNN Lineage: From Slow-and-Accurate to Fast-and-Accurate

questions.prompt: What does a detector output that a classifier doesn't?
options: A single label for the whole image
A text caption describing the scene
A class label for every pixel
Boxes, each with class and confidence
questions.explanation: Detection keeps spatial information as boxes. Per-pixel labels are segmentation.

questions.prompt: When is segmentation worth its extra cost over detection?
options: Whenever there are more than two object classes
When the task needs pixel precision
When the model must run in real time
Whenever the images are in colour
questions.explanation: A mask makes a prediction per pixel, a box only four numbers. Use segmentation when "roughly where" isn't enough.

questions.prompt: Why was the original R-CNN so slow?
options: It processed images one pixel at a time.
It ran a full CNN on ~2,000 crops per image.
It used a transformer instead of a CNN.
It retrained the network for every new image.
questions.explanation: The expensive CNN pass was repeated thousands of times. Fast R-CNN ran it once and cropped features instead.

refLinks.label: §70.2.1 The R-CNN Lineage: From Slow-and-Accurate to Fast-and-Accurate

questions.prompt: What did Faster R-CNN change from Fast R-CNN?
options: A small trainable network made the region proposals.
It added skip connections between encoder and decoder.
It dropped region proposals and predicted boxes on a grid.
It ran the CNN once on the whole image instead of per region.
questions.explanation: The Region Proposal Network replaced the external, non-learned proposal step. Running the CNN once was Fast R-CNN's change, and grid prediction is YOLO.

refLinks.label: §70.2.1 The R-CNN Lineage: From Slow-and-Accurate to Fast-and-Accurate

options: It proposes regions, then classifies each one separately.
It slides a classifier across the image at many scales.
It segments every pixel, then draws boxes around regions.
One forward pass predicts, per grid cell, a box and class.
questions.explanation: Single-shot detection skips the proposal stage, trading some accuracy on small or overlapping objects for speed.

questions.prompt: A robot needs detection at 30 frames a second, and objects are large and sparse. Which family fits?
options: A U-Net segmentation model
Single-shot (YOLO family)
Original R-CNN with selective search
Two-stage (Faster R-CNN family)
questions.explanation: Real-time with large, sparse objects is where single-shot detectors are the usual choice. Two-stage favours small, dense objects when latency allows.

questions.prompt: What problem do U-Net's skip connections solve?
options: They let the network run several kernel sizes in parallel.
They reduce the number of parameters in the decoder.
They reinject fine spatial detail lost while downsampling.
They stop gradients vanishing in very deep networks.
questions.explanation: Encoder features at each scale are concatenated into the decoder at the same scale. Vanishing gradients are what ResNet's skips fix.

questions.prompt: How do U-Net's skip connections differ mechanically from ResNet's?
options: U-Net adds features. ResNet concatenates them.
U-Net's skips run backwards from decoder to encoder.
U-Net concatenates across stages. ResNet adds.
They are identical, applied to different tasks.
questions.explanation: Same name, different job. U-Net stacks channels from early and late stages. ResNet sums the identity with the block's output.

questions.prompt: Box A is (0, 0, 4, 4) and box B is (2, 2, 6, 6), as (x1, y1, x2, y2). What is their IoU? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The overlap is 2 × 2 = 4. Each box is 16, so the union is 16 + 16 − 4 = 28. IoU = 4 / 28 = 0.143.

questions.prompt: What IoU threshold commonly counts a detection as correct?
options: Exactly 1.0, a perfect match
Above 0.95 for all tasks
Above 0.1, since any overlap counts
Above 0.5, or 0.7+ if strict
questions.explanation: 0.5 is the usual threshold. Medical and precise robotics tasks often need 0.7 or more.

questions.prompt: What is Procedure 70.2's common mistake with non-max suppression?
options: Keeping the highest-scoring box in each cluster
Using IoU to compare overlapping boxes
Running it across classes instead of per class
Sorting boxes by confidence before suppressing
questions.explanation: Run NMS per class. The other three are what Listing 70.2 does.

questions.prompt: The simplified detector's mean IoU was 0.878, with every test image above 0.5. How does the chapter read that?
options: Weak, since a mean below 0.9 fails the standard threshold
Meaningless, since IoU only applies to segmentation
Strong: it clears even the stricter 0.7 line.
A sign of overfitting, since every image passed
questions.explanation: 0.878 clears both the 0.5 and 0.7 thresholds on this controlled task. IoU applies to boxes and masks.

questions.prompt: U-Net's IoU was 0.9997 with skips and 0.9719 without. How much IoU did the skips add? Give four decimal places.
questions.explanation: 0.9997 − 0.9719 = 0.0278. The only difference was the skip connections.

questions.prompt: The skip-connection gain was modest here. When does the chapter expect it to grow?
options: On smaller images, where downsampling loses less
Never, since 0.03 IoU is the most skips can add
On tasks with fewer classes, where masks are simpler
On tasks that need finer boundaries
questions.explanation: Without skips, boundaries must be rebuilt from the coarse bottleneck. The more precise the boundary needed, the more that costs.

bookExercises.prompt: Define detection and segmentation in one sentence each, and state what spatial information both keep that whole-image classification discards.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Detection: predicts a set of bounding boxes, each with a class label and confidence score, localising objects to rectangles. Segmentation: predicts a label for every individual pixel, producing a full mask. Both keep spatial location information that whole-image classification discards entirely (a single label with no "where").

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why U-Net's skip connections and ResNet's skip connections, despite sharing a name, solve different problems.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: ResNet's skip connections add two paths at the SAME resolution to fix vanishing gradients, letting a block default to the identity function. U-Net's skip connections concatenate (not add) features from DIFFERENT stages, early fine-detail encoder features and later coarse decoder features, to reinject spatial detail lost during downsampling. Same "shortcut" shape, different mechanism and different problem.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's detector results (mean IoU 0.878, 100% of images above the 0.5 threshold), explain why "100% above 0.5" and "mean IoU 0.878" are both useful numbers to report together rather than either alone.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "100% above 0.5" alone doesn't reveal how much above 0.5. A detector could clear the threshold by a hair on every image and still report 100%, or clear it comfortably; mean IoU (0.878) fills in that missing detail, showing the typical overlap is well above the bare minimum threshold. Conversely, mean IoU alone doesn't reveal whether that average is pulled up by a few excellent detections while some images fail the correctness threshold entirely; "100% above 0.5" confirms every single image individually cleared the bar, not just the average. Together they rule out both failure modes a single number alone could hide.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the U-Net ablation's measured Dice/IoU gap (+0.0142 / +0.0278 favouring skip connections), explain in your own words why this gap is architecturally attributable to spatial detail specifically, rather than simply "more parameters," referring to what changes between the two configurations.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The only difference between the two U-Net configurations is the presence of skip connections. Encoder depth, decoder depth, parameter count in each stage, and training procedure are all held identical, so any measured difference in output quality is attributable specifically to what skip connections provide: reinjecting the encoder's fine-resolution features directly into the decoder at matching spatial scales. Since the decoder's bottleneck-only path (without skips) has to reconstruct boundary detail purely from a heavily downsampled representation that necessarily lost fine spatial information, the gap (+0.0142 Dice, +0.0278 IoU) reflects specifically the value of that reinjected spatial detail, not a generic "more capacity helps" effect, since the two configurations don't differ in overall model capacity in the way two differently-sized models would.

bookExercises.prompt: A team building a real-time video analytics pipeline for a warehouse robot is deciding between a Faster R-CNN-style detector and a YOLO-style detector. Using Procedure 70.3 and this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you'd say to help them decide.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Given that this is real-time video for warehouse robotics, per Procedure 70.3, single-shot (YOLO-style) detection is very likely the right family. Real-time inference is the binding constraint here, not maximum possible accuracy, and single-shot's speed advantage is exactly suited to that. This trade-off is worth accepting unless the warehouse's objects are unusually small, dense, or overlapping, in which case it's worth measuring whether YOLO's accuracy trade-off is actually acceptable for your specific detection targets before committing."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 70.2 warns against running NMS across classes together. Describe a concrete scenario, using the "correctly detected cat and dog with overlapping boxes" example, where running NMS across all classes at once would produce a wrong result.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: If a detector correctly identifies a cat and a dog standing close together with genuinely overlapping bounding boxes, running NMS across all classes at once would treat the dog's high-confidence box as a suppressor of the cat's box (or vice versa, whichever has lower confidence) purely because their boxes overlap above the IoU threshold, incorrectly discarding one of the two genuinely-correct, different-class detections. Running NMS separately within each class only compares cat-boxes against other cat-boxes and dog-boxes against other dog-boxes, so the legitimately overlapping but differently-classed detections never suppress each other.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about mean Average Precision (mAP), the standard detection benchmark metric that goes beyond a single IoU threshold. Explain in your own words why averaging precision across multiple IoU thresholds (e.g. 0.5 to 0.95) gives a more complete picture of detector quality than this chapter's single "IoU > 0.5" threshold alone.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A single "IoU > 0.5" threshold treats every detection above that line as equally "correct," collapsing a barely-passing 0.51 IoU detection and a nearly-perfect 0.95 IoU detection into the same pass/fail bucket, hiding real differences in localisation quality. mAP averaged across multiple IoU thresholds (typically 0.5 to 0.95 in COCO's convention) instead rewards a detector more for tighter, more precise boxes, since a detector that only clears the loosest threshold (0.5) but fails stricter ones (0.75, 0.9) scores lower under mAP than a detector whose boxes are consistently tight enough to clear even the strict thresholds, giving a much finer-grained, more complete picture of localisation quality than one binary threshold provides.
